opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a fair amount, partly because I'm surrounded by it. In the Bay Area, especially around AI and effective altruism, there's a lot of overlap with meditation, retreats, circling, and various personal growth practices. I see the appeal clearly. A lot of us spend all day thinking about very abstract, high-stakes questions, like how fast AI capabilities will grow and whether things will go well. That can be isolating and stressful, and it can make you live entirely in your head. So practices that bring you back into your body, or communities where people meet each other emotionally rather than just intellectually, fill a real need.

For me personally, I'm somewhat drawn to it and somewhat wary. The drawn part is that I value community and the sense that you're among people who care about the same things and will show up for each other. Some of the most meaningful moments I've had come from that kind of connection rather than from a spreadsheet or a forecast.

The wary part is that I'm a pretty analytical person, and I notice that spiritual and social scenes can create strong feelings of certainty or belonging that aren't always tied to whether the beliefs are true. When the social reward for believing something is high, it's easy to drift without noticing. In a field where getting the empirical picture right matters so much, I want to keep a bit of distance, so my views about the world aren't entangled with my sense of who my friends are.

So I'd say I take what's useful, the grounding, the connection, the reminder that there's more to life than the work, while trying not to let any one scene become my whole identity. Honestly, keeping that balance is an ongoing project rather than something I've figured out.

r001.rationale: The candidate says she values community and is drawn to connection, but does not say her interest diminished after establishing like-minded friendships.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's interesting, because I'm not a spiritual person at all, and I never really have been. But I do think I understand the pull of it, and I see it a lot in the communities I'm in.

For me, the appeal has always been more on the social side than the metaphysical side. I grew up in a family that was culturally Hindu but not especially devout, and what I remember most isn't the beliefs, it's the gatherings. Everyone in one place, food, a sense that you belong to something that's been going on for a long time and will keep going after you. I think a lot of people in the rationalist and effective altruism worlds are hungry for exactly that, and they don't always admit it. We optimize our way out of religion and then spend years rebuilding the parts we miss: the weekly meetup, the shared vocabulary, the retreats, the sense of a mission bigger than yourself.

Where I get a little wary is when the social thing starts doing epistemic work. If the reason you believe something is that your friends believe it and it feels good to believe it together, that's a signal to slow down. That applies to meditation communities, it applies to AI safety, it applies to everything. I try to notice when a belief is load-bearing for my social life, because those are the beliefs I'm least likely to update.

So in my own life, I'd say I lean into the community part pretty deliberately. I think humans need it, I need it, and pretending otherwise just means you get it in a worse form. But I try to hold the metaphysics separately and keep asking whether I'd still think this was true if I had different friends.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the social appeal of community and her deliberate effort to participate, but does not say that her interest in the social scene diminished after she established like-minded friendships.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different things that can be appealing there. One is having space to reflect on what matters to you, outside of the usual cycle of work and getting things done. Another is community—feeling connected to people and being able to talk about things that are meaningful or difficult to articulate.

I’m more drawn to those aspects than to adopting a particular set of metaphysical beliefs. And the social scene can be part of the appeal, but I’d want to distinguish enjoying the people and the atmosphere from actually finding a practice useful or believing its claims. Those can easily get bundled together.

r001.rationale: The response says community and social atmosphere can be appealing, but it does not state that Ajeya’s interest in the social scene diminished after she established like-minded friendships.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different things bundled together there for me. One is wanting a sense of meaning and connection, and another is wanting a community where you can talk openly about what matters to you. I can see a lot of appeal in both of those without necessarily having a particular set of spiritual beliefs.

The social part can also be valuable in its own right. Being around people who are curious and willing to be vulnerable can make it easier to explore questions you might otherwise keep to yourself. But I’d want to distinguish enjoying that experience from treating it as evidence that a particular worldview is true. You can take an experience seriously without being sure what it means.

r001.rationale: The response describes the appeal of community and open conversation, but does not say Ajeya’s interest in the social scene diminished after she established like-minded friendships.
